title: Quantifying Mixed-state Entanglement Via Partial Transpose And Realignment Moments
authors: Poetri Sonya Tarabunga And Tobias Haug
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2194 (2026).

Entanglement plays a crucial role in quantum information science and many-body physics, yet quantifying it in mixed quantum many-body systems has remained a notoriously difficult problem. Here, we introduce families of quantitative entanglement witnesses, constructed from partial transpose and realignment moments, which provide rigorous bounds on entanglement monotones as well as entanglement dimensionality. Our witnesses can be efficiently measured using SWAP tests or variants of Bell measurements, thus making them directly implementable on current hardware. Leveraging our witnesses, we present several novel results on entanglement properties of mixed states, both in quantum information and many-body physics. We develop efficient algorithms to test whether mixed states with bounded entropy have low or high entanglement, which previously was only possible for pure states. We also provide an efficient algorithm to test the Schmidt rank using only two-copy measurements, and the operator Schmidt rank using four-copy measurements. Further, our witnesses robustly certify the quantum circuit depth in the presence of noise, as well as the Schmidt rank of mixed states. Finally, we show that the entanglement phase diagram of Haar random states, quantified by the partial transpose negativity, can be fully established solely by computing our witness, a result that also applies to any state [MATH]-design. Our witnesses can also be efficiently computed for matrix product states, thus enabling the characterization of entanglement in extensive many-body systems. Finally, we make progress on the entanglement required for quantum cryptography, establishing rigorous limits on pseudoentanglement and pseudorandom density matrices with bounded entropy. Our work opens new avenues for quantifying entanglement in large and noisy quantum systems.

.
tldr: The paper introduces efficiently measurable entanglement witnesses from partial transpose and realignment moments, yielding bounds on entanglement monotones, dimensionality, and many-body entanglement properties.
motivation: Quantifying entanglement in mixed quantum many-body systems is notoriously difficult, especially with limited measurement capabilities.
method: It constructs families of quantitative entanglement witnesses based on partial transpose and realignment moments that can be measured via SWAP tests or Bell measurement variants.
result: The witnesses provide rigorous bounds on entanglement monotones and dimensionality, enable entropy-bounded entanglement tests, Schmidt-rank certification, noise-robust circuit-depth certification, and entanglement phase-diagram characterization, and imply limits on pseudoentanglement and pseudorandom density matrices.
conclusion: This work opens new avenues for quantifying entanglement in large noisy quantum systems and connects entanglement quantification to quantum cryptography and many-body physics.

title: Violation Of Bell Inequalities In 2 × 3 ...
authors: Paweł Caban And Paweł Horodecki
abstract: We consider the Clauser–Horne (CH) inequality for a qubit–qutrit system. We derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for the violation of the inequality as well as some simple sufficient conditions. Remarkably, we demonstrate the importance of local parameters in violation of the inequality. In other words, there are some families of mixed states violating the inequality for which the correlation part alone is useless in the CH test.
tldr: The paper derives necessary and sufficient conditions for violating the Clauser-Horne inequality in qubit-qutrit systems and shows that local parameters can be crucial for detecting nonlocality in mixed states.
motivation: Bell inequality violation is a key resource for device-independent quantum information tasks, yet the role of local parameters in the Clauser-Horne test for mixed-dimensional systems is not fully understood.
method: The authors analytically study the Clauser-Horne inequality for two-qudit systems with dimensions 2 and 3, deriving necessary and sufficient conditions for violation along with simpler sufficient conditions, and separating correlation and local-parameter contributions.
result: They identify families of mixed states that violate the inequality even though the correlation part alone is insufficient for the Clauser-Horne test, highlighting the importance of local parameters.
conclusion: The findings refine the understanding of nonlocality in qubit-qutrit systems and may inform the design of Bell tests and device-independent protocols with mixed-dimensional systems.

title: Spatial Structure Of Multipartite Entanglement At Measurement Induced Phase Transitions
authors: James Allen And William Witczak-Krempa
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2211 (2026).

We study multiparty entanglement near measurement induced phase transitions (MIPTs), which arise in ensembles of local quantum circuits built with unitaries and measurements. In contrast to equilibrium quantum critical transitions, where entanglement is short-ranged, MIPTs possess long-range k-party genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) characterized by an infinite hierarchy of entanglement exponents for k[MATH]2. First, we represent the average spread of entanglement with "entanglement clusters", and use them to conjecture general exponent relations: 1) classical dominance, 2) monotonicity, 3) subadditivity. We then introduce measure-weighted graphs to construct such clusters in general circuits. Second, we obtain the exact entanglement exponents for a 1d MIPT in a measurement-only circuit that maps to percolation by exploiting non-unitary conformal field theory. The exponents, which we numerically verify, obey the inequalities. We also extend the construction to a 2d MIPT that maps to classical 3d percolation, and numerically find the first entanglement exponents. Our results provide a firm ground to understand the multiparty entanglement of MIPTs, and more general ensembles of quantum circuits.

.
tldr: The paper characterizes multiparty entanglement near measurement-induced phase transitions using entanglement clusters and exact exponents from non-unitary CFT and percolation mappings.
motivation: MIPTs exhibit long-range multiparty entanglement unlike equilibrium criticality, but its spatial structure and scaling exponents remained poorly understood.
method: The authors introduce entanglement clusters and measure-weighted graphs to represent average entanglement spread, and compute exact exponents for measurement-only circuits mapping to percolation via non-unitary CFT, supported by numerics.
result: They conjecture exponent relations (classical dominance, monotonicity, subadditivity) and obtain exact 1d exponents verified numerically, plus first 2d exponents for a 3d percolation mapping.
conclusion: The results provide a framework for multiparty entanglement in MIPTs and more general ensembles of quantum circuits.

title: Detection Of A Rényi Index Dependent Transition In Entanglement Entropy Scaling
authors: Hatem Barghathi And Adrian Del Maestro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2184 (2026).

The scaling of entanglement with subsystem size encodes key information about phases and criticality, but the von Neumann entropy is costly to access in experiments and simulations, often requiring full state tomography. The second Rényi entropy is readily measured using two-copy protocols and is often used as a proxy for the von Neumann entanglement entropy, where it is assumed to track its asymptotic scaling. Sugino and Korepiny (Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 32, 1850306 (2018)) revealed that in the ground state of some highly constrained spin models, the scaling of the von Neumann and Rényi entropies can differ, varying from power law to logarithmic scaling as a function of the Rényi index. Here, we construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to the case of interacting fermions. We introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies that can provide a protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.

.
tldr: The paper constructs a number-conserving many-body state that exhibits a Rényi-index-dependent transition in the leading scaling of entanglement entropy, generalizing prior results to interacting fermions and providing a symmetry-aware lower bound from charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
motivation: The von Neumann entropy is experimentally and numerically costly, so the second Rényi entropy is often used as a proxy, but its scaling can differ from von Neumann scaling in constrained spin models. The work aims to generalize this anomalous behavior to interacting fermions and offer an experimentally accessible diagnostic.
method: The authors explicitly build a number-conserving many-body state and analyze the subsystem-size scaling of its von Neumann and Rényi entropies for different Rényi indices. They derive a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy using charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
result: They demonstrate a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, including transitions between power-law and logarithmic behavior, in an interacting fermion setting. The charge-resolved bound can detect such anomalous scaling from quantities accessible in two-copy measurement protocols.
conclusion: Rényi entropies do not always track von Neumann entanglement scaling, so care is needed when using them as proxies. Charge-resolved Rényi entropies provide a practical protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling in experiments and simulations.

title: Gibbs State Preparation For Commuting Hamiltonian: Mapping To Classical Gibbs Sampling
authors: Yeongwoo Hwang And Jiaqing Jiang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2209 (2026).

Gibbs state preparation, or Gibbs sampling, is a key computational technique extensively used in physics, statistics, and other scientific fields. Recent efforts for designing fast mixing Gibbs samplers for quantum Hamiltonians have largely focused on commuting local Hamiltonians (CLHs), a non-trivial subclass of Hamiltonians which include highly entangled systems such as the Toric code and quantum double model. Most previous Gibbs samplers relied on simulating the Davies generator, which is a Lindbladian associated with the thermalization process in nature. Instead of using the Davies generator, we design a different Gibbs sampler for various CLHs by giving a reduction to classical Hamiltonians, in the sense that one can efficiently prepare the Gibbs state for some CLH [MATH] on a quantum computer as long as one can efficiently do classical Gibbs sampling for the corresponding classical Hamiltonian [MATH]. We demonstrate that our Gibbs sampler is able to replicate state-of-the-art results as well as prepare the Gibbs state in regimes which were previously unknown, such as the low temperature region, as long as there exists fast mixing Gibbs samplers for the corresponding classical Hamiltonians. Our reductions are as follows. – If [MATH] is a 2-local qudit CLH, then [MATH] is a 2-local qudit classical Hamiltonian. – If [MATH] is a 4-local qubit CLH on 2D lattice and there are no classical qubits, then [MATH] is a 2-local qudit classical Hamiltonian on a planar graph. As an example, our algorithm can prepare the Gibbs state for the (defected) Toric code at any non-zero temperature in [MATH] time. – If [MATH] is a 4-local qubit CLH on 2D lattice and there are classical qubits, assuming that quantum terms are uniformly correctable, then [MATH] is a constant-local classical Hamiltonian.

.
tldr: The paper designs a quantum Gibbs sampler for commuting local Hamiltonians by reducing them to classical Hamiltonians, enabling efficient preparation of Gibbs states whenever classical Gibbs sampling is efficient.
motivation: Gibbs state preparation is a key computational task in physics and statistics, but existing quantum samplers rely on simulating the Davies generator and are limited, especially at low temperatures.
method: The authors construct reductions from commuting local quantum Hamiltonians (e.g., 2-local qudit, 4-local qubit on 2D lattice) to classical Hamiltonians, then apply classical Gibbs sampling techniques to prepare the quantum Gibbs state.

title: Floquetifying Stabiliser Codes With Distance-preserving Rewrites
authors: Benjamin Rodatz, Boldizsár Poór, And Aleks Kissinger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2202 (2026).

Stabiliser codes with large weight measurements can be challenging to implement fault-tolerantly. To overcome this, we propose a Floquetification procedure which, given a stabiliser code, synthesises a novel Floquet code that only uses single- and two-qubit operations. Moreover, this procedure preserves the distance and number of logicals of the original code. The new Floquet code requires additional physical qubits. This overhead is linear in the weight of the largest measurement of the original code. Our method is based on the ZX calculus, a graphical language for representing and rewriting quantum circuits. However, a problem arises with the use of ZX in the context of rewriting error-correcting codes: ZX rewrites generally do not preserve code distance. Tackling this issue, we define the notion of distance-preserving rewrite that enables the transformation of error-correcting codes without changing their distance. These distance-preserving rewrites are used to decompose arbitrary weight stabiliser measurements into quantum circuits with single- and two-qubit operations. As we only use distance-preserving rewrites, we are guaranteed that a single error in the resulting circuit creates at most a single error on the data qubits. These decompositions enable us to generalise the Floquetification procedure of Townsend-Teague et al [83] to arbitrary stabiliser codes, provably preserving the distance and number of logicals of the original code.

.
tldr: A procedure that transforms arbitrary stabiliser codes into Floquet codes using distance-preserving ZX rewrites, preserving code distance and logical qubit count at linear qubit overhead.
motivation: Stabiliser codes with high-weight measurements are difficult to implement fault-tolerantly, and existing Floquetification methods are limited to specific code families.
method: The authors use ZX calculus to define distance-preserving rewrites, which decompose arbitrary-weight stabiliser measurements into single- and two-qubit operations, then synthesise a Floquet code from the rewritten circuit.
result: The resulting Floquet code uses only single- and two-qubit operations, preserves the distance and number of logical qubits of the original code, and requires an overhead linear in the largest measurement weight.
conclusion: The work generalises Floquetification to arbitrary stabiliser codes with provable distance preservation, enabling more practical fault-tolerant implementations.

title: Simple Logical Quantum Computation With Concatenated Symplectic Double Codes
authors: Noah Berthusen And Elijah Durso-Sabina
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2195 (2026).

There have been significant recent advances in constructing theoretical and practical quantum error correcting codes that function well as quantum memories; however, performing fault-tolerant logical gates on these codes is less studied, and the protocols that do exist often require significant complexity. Building off the symplectic double construction, we investigate concatenated symplectic double codes, which have a rich set of logical gates implementable using only physical single-qubit gates and qubit relabeling. Combined with injected fold-transversal gates, the full Clifford group on a single codeblock is achieved through a functionally simple circuit. We perform circuit-level simulations of state preparation and quantum error correction on these codes and show that they have promising performance at near state-of-the-art physical error rates. As such, we argue that concatenated symplectic double codes are strong contenders as the underlying computational code on medium- to large-scale quantum computers.

.
tldr: Investigates concatenated symplectic double codes for implementing logical gates with simple physical operations, showing promising performance for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
motivation: Fault-tolerant logical gates on quantum error correcting codes are less studied and existing protocols often require significant complexity, motivating the search for simpler gate implementations.
method: The authors study concatenated symplectic double codes, which enable logical gates via single-qubit gates and qubit relabeling, combined with injected fold-transversal gates to achieve the full Clifford group, and perform circuit-level simulations of state preparation and error correction.
result: The codes achieve the full Clifford group on a single codeblock with a functionally simple circuit and demonstrate promising performance at near state-of-the-art physical error rates.
conclusion: Concatenated symplectic double codes are strong contenders as the underlying computational code for medium- to large-scale quantum computers.

title: Catalytic $z$-rotations In Constant $T$-depth
authors: Isaac H. Kim
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2191 (2026).

We show that the [MATH]-depth of any single-qubit [MATH]-rotation can be reduced to [MATH] if a certain catalyst state is available. To achieve an [MATH]-approximation, it suffices to have a catalyst state of size polynomial in [MATH]. This implies that [MATH] admits a finite universal gate set consisting of Clifford+[MATH]. In particular, there are catalytic constant [MATH]-depth circuits that approximate multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform arbitrarily well. We also show that the catalyst state can be prepared in time polynomial in [MATH].

.
tldr: Kim shows that with a suitable catalyst state, any single-qubit z-rotation can be implemented in constant T-depth, enabling constant-depth approximations of Toffoli, adders, and QFT.
motivation: T-depth is a central cost metric in fault-tolerant quantum computing, and reducing it for arbitrary rotations is important for efficient quantum algorithms.
method: The paper uses catalytic quantum states and Clifford+T circuits to implement z-rotations in constant T-depth, with a catalyst state whose size is polynomial in the approximation parameter and which can be prepared efficiently.
result: Any single-qubit z-rotation can be epsilon-approximated with constant T-depth using a polynomial-size catalyst, yielding a finite universal gate set and constant T-depth circuits for multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform.
conclusion: Catalytic constant T-depth computation is feasible, potentially reducing resource requirements for fault-tolerant implementations of key quantum algorithms.

title: Entanglement Growth In The Dark Intervals Of A Locally Monitored Free-fermion Chain
authors: Giovanni Di Fresco, Youenn Le Gal, Davide Valenti, Marco Schiró, And Angelo Carollo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2183 (2026).

We consider a free fermionic chain with monitoring of the particle density on a single site of the chain and study the entanglement dynamics of quantum jump trajectories. We show that the entanglement entropy grows in time towards a stationary state which display volume law scaling of the entropy, in stark contrast with both the unitary dynamics after a local quench and the no-click limit corresponding to full post-selection. We explain the extensive entanglement growth as a consequence of the peculiar distribution of quantum jumps in time, which display superpoissonian waiting time distribution characterised by a bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals where no-clicks are detected, akin to the distribution of fluorescence light in a driven atom. We show that the presence of dark intervals is the key feature to explain the effect and that by increasing the number of sites which are monitored the volume law scaling gives away to the Zeno effect and its associated area law.

.
tldr: Monitoring a single site in a free-fermion chain leads to volume-law entanglement growth driven by clustered quantum jumps and long dark intervals, while monitoring more sites induces a Zeno-effect area law.
motivation: The paper studies how local monitoring and quantum jump trajectories affect entanglement scaling, contrasting with unitary dynamics and the no-click limit.
method: They simulate quantum jump trajectories for a free-fermionic chain with particle-density monitoring on one site and analyze the entanglement entropy, waiting-time statistics, and scaling with the number of monitored sites.
result: Entanglement entropy grows extensively toward a volume-law stationary state due to super-Poissonian jump bunching and dark intervals; increasing monitored sites suppresses this via the Zeno effect into area-law scaling.
conclusion: Dark intervals between quantum jumps are the key mechanism for the observed entanglement growth, and the transition from volume to area law is controlled by the number of monitored sites.

title: Breaking The Orthogonality Barrier In Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Kenta Kasai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2205 (2026).

Classical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are a widely deployed and well-established technology, forming the backbone of modern communication and storage systems. It is well known that, in this classical setting, increasing the girth of the Tanner graph while maintaining regular degree distributions leads simultaneously to good belief-propagation (BP) decoding performance and large minimum distance. In the quantum setting, however, this principle does not directly apply because quantum LDPC codes must satisfy additional orthogonality constraints between their parity-check matrices. When one enforces both orthogonality and regularity in a straightforward manner, the girth is typically reduced and the minimum distance becomes structurally upper bounded. In this work, we overcome this limitation by using permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and by restricting the orthogonality constraints to only the active part of the construction, while preserving regular check-matrix structures. This design circumvents conventional structural distance limitations induced by parent-matrix orthogonality, and enables the construction of quantum LDPC codes with large girth while avoiding latent low-weight logical operators. As a concrete demonstration, we construct a girth-8, (3,12)-regular [MATH] quantum LDPC code and show that, under BP decoding combined with a low-complexity post-processing algorithm, it achieves a frame error rate as low as [MATH] on the depolarizing channel with error probability [MATH].

.
tldr: A novel construction of quantum LDPC codes that breaks the orthogonality barrier by using controlled-commutativity permutation matrices, achieving large girth and good BP decoding performance.
motivation: Quantum LDPC codes require orthogonality between parity-check matrices, which typically reduces Tanner graph girth and structurally bounds minimum distance, limiting BP decoding performance.
method: The author employs permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and restricts orthogonality constraints to only the active part of the construction while preserving regular check-matrix structures.
result: A girth-8, (3,12)-regular quantum LDPC code is constructed, and under BP decoding with low-complexity post-processing it achieves a frame error rate as low as 10^-5 on the depolarizing channel at error probability 0.1.
conclusion: The approach circumvents conventional structural distance limitations, enabling quantum LDPC codes with large girth and no latent low-weight logical operators, thus advancing practical quantum error correction.

title: Streaming Belief Propagation On Mixed-Alphabet Tanner Graphs For Practical Quantum Memory
authors: Kao-Yueh Kuo And Ching-Yi Lai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2207 (2026).

Reliable quantum memory under circuit-level noise requires decoders that can process syndrome information continuously and at a rate comparable to its generation. In practical quantum error correction (QEC), repeated syndrome measurements cause the number of potential error locations to grow rapidly with both code size and time. In this paper, we propose a streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation (SM-BP) decoder. We construct a space-time Tanner graph across multiple rounds of syndrome extraction with mixed-alphabet error variables, preserving correlations arising from multi-qubit faults. Additionally, we propose an adaptive sliding window procedure that captures long error events across window boundaries and adjusts the decoding in real time. To enhance SM-BP, we introduce a technique of probabilistic error consolidation to mitigate degeneracy effects and short cycles. Our simulations demonstrate high error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% and strong error-floor performance for topological code families, including rotated toric, toric color, and twisted XZZX toric codes. These results show that SM-BP provides a practical decoding framework for continuous QEC under circuit-level noise.

.
tldr: Proposes a streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation decoder for practical quantum memory under circuit-level noise.
motivation: Reliable quantum memory requires decoders that continuously process syndrome information at rates comparable to its generation, but repeated measurements cause error locations to grow rapidly with code size and time.
method: Constructs a space-time Tanner graph with mixed-alphabet error variables, uses an adaptive sliding window to capture long error events, and introduces probabilistic error consolidation to mitigate degeneracy and short cycles.
result: Simulations show high error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% and strong error-floor performance for rotated toric, toric color, and twisted XZZX toric codes.
conclusion: SM-BP provides a practical decoding framework for continuous quantum error correction under circuit-level noise.

title: Information Gain And Measurement Disturbance For Quantum Agents
authors: Arthur O T Pang, Noah Lupu-Gladstein, Y Batuhan Yilmaz, C Pria Dobney, Rui Jie Tang, Aharon Brodutch And Aephraim M Steinberg
abstract: The traditional formalism of quantum measurement (hereafter ‘TQM’) describes processes where some properties of quantum states are extracted and stored as classical information. While TQM is a natural and appropriate description of how humans interact with quantum systems, it is silent on the question of how a more general, quantum, agent would do so. How do we describe the observation of a system by an agent with the ability to store not only classical information but quantum states in its memory? In this paper, we extend the idea of measurement to a more general class of sensors for quantum agents which interact with a system in such a way that the agent’s memory stores information (classical or quantum) about the system under study. For appropriate sensory interactions, the quantum agent may ‘learn’ more about the system than would be possible under any set of classical measurements—but as we show, this comes at the cost of additional measurement disturbance. We experimentally demonstrate such a system and characterize the tradeoffs by considering the channel capacity required to erase the effect of a measurement.
tldr: The paper generalizes quantum measurement to quantum agents with quantum memory, showing that quantum memory can yield more information about a system than classical measurements, but at the cost of additional disturbance, and experimentally characterizes the tradeoff via the channel capacity needed to erase the measurement's effect.
motivation: Traditional quantum measurement formalism assumes that the observer stores only classical information, so it cannot describe how an agent with quantum memory would observe a quantum system. This raises the fundamental question of how information gain and disturbance trade off for quantum agents.
method: The authors extend the notion of measurement to a general class of sensors for quantum agents whose memory can store classical or quantum information about the system. They experimentally demonstrate such a system and quantify the tradeoffs by considering the channel capacity required to erase the effect of a measurement.
result: For appropriate sensory interactions, a quantum agent can learn more about the system than any set of classical measurements, but this advantage comes at the cost of additional measurement disturbance. The tradeoff is experimentally characterized.
conclusion: The work broadens measurement theory to quantum agents with quantum memory, revealing a novel information-disturbance tradeoff and quantifying it through erasure channel capacity.

title: Reducing Spatial And Temporal Dimensionality In The Multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett Model
authors: Hongfei Zhan, Ernest W.Z. Pan, And Zhenning Cai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2201 (2026).

Focusing on the real-time dynamics of the reduced density matrix of the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model, several techniques are adopted in this paper to reduce the spatial and temporal dimensionality, combined into an efficient algorithm. From a spatial perspective, an equivalent formulation of the Dyson series is presented. With the aid of a low-rank approximation, the spatial dimensionality of open quantum system simulations is halved. From a temporal perspective, the frozen Gaussian approximation is used to approximate both the evolution operator and the interaction operator in the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model. This reduces the high-dimensional integrals to one- and two-dimensional integrals independent of the truncation level of the Dyson series. Through these techniques, we design an efficient algorithm whose validity is verified through several numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional double slit simulation.

.
tldr: The paper develops an efficient algorithm for simulating the real-time dynamics of the reduced density matrix in the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model by reducing both spatial and temporal dimensionality.
motivation: Simulating the real-time dynamics of multidimensional open quantum systems is computationally challenging due to high-dimensional integrals and large spatial grids, especially for the Caldeira-Leggett model which is central to understanding decoherence and quantum Brownian motion.
method: The authors introduce an equivalent Dyson series formulation combined with a low-rank approximation to halve the spatial dimensionality, and employ the frozen Gaussian approximation to reduce high-dimensional temporal integrals to one- and two-dimensional integrals independent of the Dyson series truncation level.
result: The resulting algorithm is validated through numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional double-slit simulation, demonstrating its efficiency and accuracy for multidimensional open quantum system dynamics.
conclusion: The proposed dimensionality reduction techniques enable efficient simulation of the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model, making previously intractable real-time reduced density matrix calculations feasible.

title: Measurement Incompatibility In Bayesian Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
authors: Francesco Albarelli, Dominic Branford, And Jesús Rubio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2192 (2026).

We present a comprehensive and pedagogical formulation of Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation. Within this framework, we analyse the role of measurement incompatibility and establish its quantitative effect on attainable precision. We achieve this by deriving upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement – a notion from hypothesis testing – combined with the evaluation of the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. In general, we prove that, as in the many-copy regime of local estimation theory, incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the idealised scenario in which individually optimal measurements are assumed jointly implementable. Therefore, in practical situations, the latter may provide a sufficient and computationally efficient benchmark without solving the full optimisation problem. Our results, which we illustrate through applications of discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing, provide analytical and numerical tools for assessing ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, including an open-source package for all the bounds discussed here.

.
tldr: This paper formulates Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation and quantifies how measurement incompatibility limits attainable precision, showing it can at most double the minimum loss relative to jointly implementable optimal measurements.
motivation: Measurement incompatibility is a fundamental quantum resource, but its quantitative role in Bayesian multiparameter estimation was not fully understood. The authors aim to provide a comprehensive framework and practical bounds for assessing ultimate precision limits.
method: They derive upper bounds using the pretty good measurement from hypothesis testing and evaluate the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. Applications to discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing illustrate the approach, with an open-source package for all bounds.
result: They prove that, as in many-copy local estimation, incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the idealised scenario with jointly implementable individually optimal measurements. This implies the idealised benchmark is often sufficient and computationally efficient.
conclusion: The work provides analytical and numerical tools to assess ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, with open-source software for practical use.

title: Disorder-Induced Entanglement Phase Transitions In Non-Hermitian Systems With Skin Effects
authors: Kai Li, Ze-Chuan Liu, And Yong Xu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2186 (2026).

Non-Hermitian dynamics is ubiquitous in various physical systems. While recent study shows that such a dynamics leads to an area-law scaling of the entanglement entropy due to the non-Hermitian skin effects, it remains unclear how disorder changes the behavior of the entanglement entropy in a non-Hermitian system with skin effects. Here we study the dynamics of a many-body state of free fermions in the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model with open boundaries, and find that the area-law behavior of the entanglement entropy in the pristine Hatano-Nelson model develops into a logarithmic scaling for small disorder strength. As we further increase the disorder strength, the system reenters an area-law regime through an entanglement phase transition. At the critical point, the entanglement entropy exhibits a universal algebraic scaling. We further demonstrate the absence of a conformal invariance in the log-law regime by examining the subsystem entanglement entropy, the connected correlation function and the mutual information. Finally, we show the existence of disorder induced entanglement phase transitions in the Hatano-Nelson model with periodic boundaries.

.
tldr: Disorder drives an area-law to logarithmic to area-law entanglement phase transition in the non-Hermitian Hatano-Nelson model with skin effects.
motivation: The non-Hermitian skin effect is known to produce area-law entanglement, but how disorder modifies entanglement scaling in such systems was unclear.
method: The authors study free-fermion many-body dynamics in the Hatano-Nelson model with open and periodic boundaries, computing entanglement entropy, connected correlation functions, and mutual information.
result: Small disorder induces logarithmic entanglement scaling, while stronger disorder drives a reentrant area-law phase via an entanglement phase transition with universal algebraic scaling at criticality; the logarithmic regime lacks conformal invariance.
conclusion: Disorder can induce entanglement phase transitions in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects, and the resulting logarithmic phase is not conformally invariant.

title: Non-secular Polariton Leakage And Dark-state Protection In Hybrid Plasmonic Cavities
authors: Marco Vallone
abstract: A major issue in exploiting plasmonic cavities as key components in nanotechnology is the effect of radiative and absorption losses on their electrodynamic behavior. Treating them as open systems, we derive a time-local, completely positive master equation that retains non-secular interference between decay pathways and reduces to the standard secular description when the environment resolves polariton splitting. When it does not, the theory predicts order-one deviations from secular leakage dynamics, including bath-induced coherences and formation of a comparatively long-lived dark polaritonic component, and provides a simple design criterion based on the ratio of polariton splitting to reservoir linewidth. A time-resolved leakage measurement, such as transmission, reflectivity, or photoluminescence, can be used to observe these effects.
tldr: Derives a non-secular master equation for open plasmonic cavities, predicting long-lived dark polaritonic states and a design criterion based on the ratio of polariton splitting to reservoir linewidth.
motivation: Plasmonic cavities suffer from radiative and absorption losses, and standard secular descriptions may fail when the environment does not resolve polariton splitting, obscuring key leakage dynamics.

title: Faster Quantum Simulation Of Markovian Open Quantum Systems Via Randomisation
authors: I.J. David, I. Sinayskiy, And F. Petruccione
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2204 (2026).

When simulating the dynamics of open quantum systems with quantum computers, it is essential to accurately approximate the system's behaviour while preserving the physicality of its evolution. Traditionally, for Markovian open quantum systems, this has been achieved using first and second-order Trotter-Suzuki product formulas or probabilistic algorithms. In this work, we introduce novel non-probabilistic algorithms for simulating Markovian open quantum systems using randomisation. Our methods, including first and second-order randomised Trotter-Suzuki formulas and the QDRIFT channel, not only maintain the physicality of the system's evolution but also enhance the scalability and precision of quantum simulations. We derive error bounds and step count limits for these techniques, bypassing the need for the mixing lemma typically employed in Hamiltonian simulation proofs. Furthermore, we implement these randomised algorithms using Classical Sampling (CS), demonstrating their gate complexity advantages over deterministic TS product formulas. This work systematically extends powerful randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to the general setting of Markovian open quantum systems, highlighting their potential to enable faster and more accurate simulations.

.
tldr: Introduces non-probabilistic randomised algorithms for simulating Markovian open quantum systems, achieving better gate complexity and error bounds than deterministic Trotter-Suzuki formulas.
motivation: Efficient quantum simulation of open quantum system dynamics requires approximations that preserve physicality while scaling well, but existing deterministic methods have high gate costs.
method: Extends randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to Markovian open quantum systems, deriving error bounds and step count limits without the mixing lemma, and implements via Classical Sampling.
result: Demonstrates gate complexity advantages over deterministic Trotter-Suzuki formulas for simulating Markovian dynamics, with rigorous error bounds.
conclusion: Randomisation techniques can enable faster and more accurate quantum simulation of open quantum systems, with potential for broader adoption.

title: Quantum Resource Comparison For Two Leading Surface Code Lattice Surgery Approaches
authors: Tyler Leblond And Ryan S. Bennink
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2187 (2026).

Hamiltonian simulation is one of the most promising candidates for the demonstration of quantum advantage within the next ten years, and several studies have proposed end-to-end resource estimates for executing such algorithms on fault-tolerant quantum processors. Usually, these resource estimates are based upon the assumption that quantum error correction is implemented using the surface code, and that the best surface code compilation scheme involves serializing input circuits by eliminating all Clifford gates. This transformation is thought to make best use of the native multi-body measurement (lattice surgery) instruction set available to surface codes. Some work, however, has suggested that direct compilation from Clifford+T to lattice surgery operations may be beneficial for circuits that have high degrees of logical parallelism. In this study, we analyze the resource costs for implementing Hamiltonian simulation using example approaches from each of these leading surface code compilation families. The Hamiltonians whose dynamics we consider are those of the transverse-field Ising model in several geometries, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the [MATH] complex under a time-varying magnetic field. We show, among other things, that the optimal scheme depends on whether Hamiltonian simulation is implemented using the quantum signal processing or Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, with Trotterization benefiting by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation for these applications. Our results suggest that surface code quantum computers should not have a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme, but that smart compilers should predict the optimal scheme based upon high-level quantities from logical circuits such as average circuit density, numbers of logical qubits, and T fraction.

.
tldr: The paper compares resource costs of two leading surface code lattice surgery compilation families for Hamiltonian simulation, showing that the optimal scheme depends on the simulation algorithm and circuit-level properties.
motivation: Fault-tolerant resource estimates for Hamiltonian simulation typically assume a single surface code compilation strategy that serializes Clifford gates, yet direct Clifford+T-to-lattice-surgery compilation may benefit highly parallel circuits.
method: End-to-end resource estimation for Hamiltonian simulation (transverse-field Ising in several geometries, Kitaev honeycomb, and a complex under time-varying magnetic field) using quantum signal processing and Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, comparing serialized Clifford and direct Clifford+T lattice surgery compilation schemes.
result: The optimal compilation scheme depends on the simulation algorithm: Trotterization gains orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation, whereas the best choice varies with circuit density, logical qubit count, and T fraction.
conclusion: Surface code quantum computers should not adopt a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme; smart compilers should predict the optimal approach from high-level logical circuit quantities.

title: Robust Topological Quantum State Transfer With Long-range Interactions In Rydberg Arrays
authors: Siri Raupach, Beatriz Olmos, And Mathias B. M. Svendsen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2190 (2026).

We develop a theoretical framework for fast, robust and high-fidelity topological quantum state transfer in one-dimensional systems with long-range couplings, motivated by chains of Rydberg atoms with dipole–dipole interactions. Such long-range interactions naturally give rise to extended Su–Schrieffer–Heeger and Rice–Mele models supporting topologically protected edge states. We show that these edge states enable high-fidelity edge-to-edge excitation transfer using both time-independent protocols, based on coherent edge state dynamics, and time-dependent protocols, based on adiabatic modulation of system parameters. Long-range couplings play a central role by enhancing the relevant energy gaps, leading to a substantial improvement in transfer efficiency compared to nearest neighbour models. The resulting transfer is robust against positional disorder, reflecting its topological origin and highlighting the potential of long-range interacting platforms for reliable quantum state transfer.

.
tldr: The authors develop a theoretical framework for fast, robust and high-fidelity topological quantum state transfer in one-dimensional long-range coupled systems, motivated by Rydberg atom chains with dipole-dipole interactions.
motivation: Rydberg atom arrays are a promising platform for quantum information processing, and reliable state transfer between distant sites is a key primitive; topological protection offers a route to robustness against disorder and imperfections.
method: They study long-range interacting extensions of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger and Rice-Mele models, using both time-independent protocols based on coherent edge-state dynamics and time-dependent adiabatic modulation of system parameters, comparing to nearest-neighbour models.
result: Long-range couplings enhance the relevant energy gaps, yielding substantially improved edge-to-edge transfer efficiency and fidelity, with robustness against positional disorder stemming from the topological origin of the edge states.
conclusion: Long-range interacting platforms such as Rydberg arrays are well suited for reliable topological quantum state transfer, suggesting interesting prospects for quantum information routing on these devices.

title: Generalising Aumann’s Agreement Theorem
authors: Matthew Leifer And Cristhiano Duarte
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2210 (2026).

According to Aumann's celebrated theorem, rational agents cannot agree to disagree. In other words, agents who once shared a common prior probability distribution and who have common knowledge about their posteriors cannot assign different probability distributions to a given proposition. Common knowledge imposes strong restrictions on assigned probabilities. In fact, Aumann's agreement theorem was one of the first attempts to formalise and explore the role played by common knowledge in decision theory. Recently, the debate over possible (quantum) extensions of Aumann's results has resurfaced. This paper contributes to this discussion. First, we argue that agreeing to disagree is impossible in quantum theory. Secondly, by building on the quantum argument, we show that agreeing to disagree is also forbidden in any generalised probability theory. The upshot is that in its probabilistic version, the agreement theorem is a direct consequence of how we choose to condition upon acquiring new information.

.
tldr: The paper generalizes Aumann's agreement theorem to quantum theory and generalised probability theories, showing that rational agents cannot agree to disagree.
motivation: Aumann's theorem formalizes common knowledge in decision theory, and recent debate over quantum extensions motivates a general probabilistic treatment.
method: The authors define common knowledge in generalised probabilistic theories using the notion of a common prior and show that the agreement theorem holds under certain conditions.

title: Quantum Max d-Cut Via Qudit Swap Operators
authors: Igor Klep, Tea Štrekelj, And Jurij Volčič
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2203 (2026).

Quantum Max Cut (QMC) problem for systems of qubits is an example of a 2-local Hamiltonian problem, and a prominent paradigm in computational complexity theory. This paper investigates the algebraic structure of a higher-dimensional analog of the QMC problem for systems of qudits. The Quantum Max [MATH]-Cut ([MATH]-QMC) problem asks for the largest eigenvalue of a Hamiltonian on a graph with [MATH] vertices whose edges correspond to swap operators acting on [MATH]. The algebra generated by the swap operators is identified as a quotient of a free algebra modulo symmetric group relations and a single additional relation of degree [MATH]. This presentation leads to a tailored hierarchy of semidefinite programs, leveraging noncommutative polynomial optimization (NPO) methods, that converges to the solution of the [MATH]-QMC problem. For a large class of complete bipartite graphs, exact solutions for the [MATH]-QMC problem are derived using the representation theory of symmetric groups and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients. Lastly, the paper addresses a refined [MATH]-QMC problem focused on finding the largest eigenvalue within each isotypic component (irreducible block) of the graph Hamiltonian. It is shown that the spectrum of the star graph Hamiltonian distinguishes between isotypic components of the [MATH]-QMC problem. For general [MATH], low-degree relations for separating isotypic components are presented, enabling adaptation of the global NPO hierarchy to efficiently compute the largest eigenvalue in each isotypic component.

.
tldr: This paper studies the algebraic structure of the Quantum Max d-Cut problem for qudits, develops a semidefinite programming hierarchy for its solution, and derives exact results for complete bipartite graphs using representation theory.
motivation: Quantum Max Cut is a prominent 2-local Hamiltonian problem in computational complexity, and its higher-dimensional qudit generalization is less understood, motivating algebraic and computational tools for solving it.
method: The authors identify the algebra generated by qudit swap operators as a quotient of a free algebra with symmetric group relations and an extra relation, then construct a tailored noncommutative polynomial optimization hierarchy of semidefinite programs and use symmetric group representation theory.
result: The hierarchy converges to the solution of d-QMC; exact solutions are obtained for a large class of complete bipartite graphs; and the star graph spectrum distinguishes isotypic components, with low-degree relations enabling efficient component-wise computation.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic algebraic and optimization framework for Quantum Max d-Cut, yielding both algorithmic convergence and representation-theoretic exact solutions for structured graphs.

title: Unconditional Quantum Advantage For Sampling With Shallow Circuits
authors: Adam Bene Watts And Natalie Parham
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2188 (2026).

Recent work by Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig showed that there exists a search problem that a constant-depth quantum circuit can solve, but that any constant-depth classical circuit with bounded fan-in cannot. They also pose the question: Can we achieve a similar proof of separation for an input-independent sampling task? In this paper, we show that the answer to this question is yes when the number of random input bits given to the classical circuit is bounded. We introduce a distribution [MATH] over [MATH] and construct a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family [MATH] such that [MATH] samples from a distribution close to [MATH] in total variation distance. For any [MATH] we also prove, unconditionally, that any classical circuit with bounded fan-in gates that takes as input [MATH] i.i.d. Bernouli random variables with entropy [MATH] and produces output close to [MATH] in total variation distance has depth [MATH]. This gives an unconditional proof that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that can't be reproduced by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits, even up to additive error. We also show a similar separation between constant-depth quantum circuits with advice and classical circuits with bounded fan-in and fan-out, but access to an unbounded number of i.i.d random inputs. The distribution [MATH] and classical circuit lower bounds are inspired by work of Viola, in which he shows a different (but related) distribution cannot be sampled from approximately by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits.

.
tldr: The paper unconditionally proves that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that cannot be approximated by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits, even with random inputs.
motivation: Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig previously showed a search-problem separation and asked whether an input-independent sampling task could achieve a similar unconditional quantum advantage. This work answers that question affirmatively.
method: The authors introduce a distribution and construct a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family that samples from a distribution close in total variation distance. They then prove a lower bound on the depth of any classical bounded fan-in circuit that takes i.i.d. Bernoulli random inputs and tries to approximate the same distribution.
result: They obtain an unconditional separation between constant-depth quantum circuits and constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits for sampling up to additive error. They also prove a similar separation between quantum circuits with advice and classical circuits with bounded fan-in and fan-out and access to an unbounded number of random inputs.
conclusion: This establishes a new unconditional quantum advantage for shallow sampling tasks, extending previous separations from search problems to input-independent sampling and strengthening the case for quantum computational advantages in low-depth regimes.

title: Non-Gaussian Noise Magnetometry Using Local Spin Qubits
authors: Jonathan B. Curtis, Amir Yacoby, And Eugene Demler
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2197 (2026).

Atomic scale qubits, as may be realized in nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, offer the opportunity to study magnetic field noise with nanometer scale spatial resolution. Using these spin qubits, one can learn a great deal about the magnetic-field noise correlations, and correspondingly the collective-mode spectra, in quantum materials and devices. However, to date these tools have been essentially restricted to studying Gaussian noise processes – equivalent to linear-response. In this work we will show how to extend these techniques beyond the Gaussian regime and show how to unambiguously measure higher-order magnetic noise cumulants in a local, spatially resolved way. We unveil two protocols for doing this; the first uses a single spin-qubit and different dynamical decoupling sequences to extract non-Markovian and non-Gaussian spin-echo noise. The second protocol uses two-qubit coincidence measurements to study spatially non-local cumulants in the magnetic noise. We then demonstrate the utility of these protocols by considering a model of a bath of non-interacting two-level systems, as well as a model involving spatially correlated magnetic fluctuations near a second-order Ising phase transition. In both cases, we highlight how this technique can be used to measure in a real many-body system how fluctuation dynamics converge towards the central limit theorem as a function of effective bath size. We then conclude by discussing some promising applications and extensions of this method.

.
tldr: The paper develops two protocols using NV-center spin qubits—dynamical-decoupling spin-echo sequences and two-qubit coincidence measurements—to extract higher-order (non-Gaussian) magnetic noise cumulants with nanometer spatial resolution.
motivation: NV-center magnetometry has so far been limited to Gaussian noise processes, equivalent to linear response, leaving higher-order correlations and collective-mode spectra in quantum materials largely inaccessible.
method: One protocol uses a single spin qubit with tailored dynamical decoupling sequences to isolate non-Markovian and non-Gaussian spin-echo noise; a second uses two-qubit coincidence measurements to probe spatially non-local noise cumulants, demonstrated on a bath of non-interacting two-level systems and on spatially correlated fluctuations near a second-order Ising transition.
result: The protocols can unambiguously measure higher-order magnetic noise cumulants locally and in a spatially resolved manner, and track how fluctuation dynamics converge to the central limit theorem as a function of effective bath size.
conclusion: The work extends NV-based noise spectroscopy beyond the Gaussian regime, offering a tool to characterize non-linear and spatially correlated fluctuations in many-body quantum materials, with further extensions discussed.

title: Sparse Quantum State Preparation With Improved Toffoli Cost
authors: Felix Rupprecht And Sabine Wölk
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2208 (2026).

The preparation of quantum states is one of the most fundamental tasks in quantum computing, and a key primitive in many quantum algorithms. Of particular interest to areas such as quantum simulation and linear-system solvers are sparse quantum states, which contain only a small number [MATH] of non-zero computational basis states compared to a generic state. In this work, we present an approach that prepares [MATH]-sparse states on [MATH] qubits, reducing the number of Toffoli gates required compared to prior art. We work in the established framework of first preparing a dense state on a [MATH]-qubit sub-register, and then mapping this state to the target state via an isometry, with the latter step dominating the cost of the full algorithm. The speed-up is achieved by designing an efficient algorithm for finding and implementing the isometry. The worst-case Toffoli cost of our isometry circuit, which may be viewed as a batched version of an approach by Malvetti et al., is essentially [MATH] for sufficiently large values of [MATH], yielding roughly a [MATH] improvement factor over the state-of-the-art. In numerical benchmarks on randomly chosen states, the cost is closer to [MATH]. With the improved isometry circuit, we examine the dense-state preparation step and present ways to optimize the joint cost of both steps, particularly in the case of target states with purely real coefficients, by outsourcing some sub-tasks from the dense-state preparation to the isometry.

.
tldr: The paper presents a circuit-construction algorithm for preparing sparse quantum states that reduces the worst-case Toffoli gate count compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches.
motivation: Sparse state preparation is a fundamental primitive for quantum simulation and linear-system solvers, and existing methods based on dense-subregister preparation plus isometry mapping are dominated by the isometry cost, so improving that step yields practical circuit savings.
method: The authors build on the framework of preparing a dense state on a small sub-register and then applying an isometry to the target state, designing an efficient algorithm for finding and implementing this isometry (a batched version of the Malvetti et al. approach) and additionally optimizing the joint cost of the dense-preparation and isometry steps, including the real-coefficient case.
result: The worst-case Toffoli cost of the isometry circuit scales essentially as O(...) for sufficiently large parameters, giving roughly a quadratic-type improvement over prior art, with numerical benchmarks on random states showing costs close to the lower bound.
conclusion: Improved isometry synthesis substantially lowers the Toffoli cost of sparse state preparation and allows better balancing between dense-state preparation and isometry, though the contribution is a circuit-compilation resource optimization rather than an information-theoretic result.

title: A Brief History Of Quantum Vs Classical Computational Advantage
authors: Ryan Larose
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2198 (2026).

In this review article we summarize all experiments claiming quantum computational advantage to date. Our review highlights challenges, loopholes, and refutations appearing in subsequent work to provide a complete picture of the current statuses of these experiments. In addition, we also discuss theoretical computational advantage in example problems such as approximate optimization and recommendation systems. Finally, we review recent experiments in quantum error correction --- the biggest frontier to reach experimental quantum advantage in Shor's algorithm.

.
tldr: A review summarizing experimental claims of quantum computational advantage, their challenges and refutations, plus related theoretical and quantum error correction developments.
motivation: To provide a complete picture of the current status of quantum advantage experiments and the obstacles to achieving practical advantage.
method: Survey of all experiments claiming quantum computational advantage, subsequent challenges, and discussion of theoretical advantage in approximate optimization and recommendation systems, along with recent QEC experiments.
result: Highlights numerous loopholes and refutations in claimed advantage experiments and reviews progress in QEC toward fault-tolerant Shor's algorithm.
conclusion: Quantum advantage remains contested; error correction is the critical frontier for reaching practical quantum advantage.

title: Quantum Phase Estimation With Optimal Confidence Interval Using Three Control Qubits
authors: Kaur Kristjuhan And Dominic W. Berry
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2193 (2026).

Quantum phase estimation is an important routine in many quantum algorithms, particularly for estimating the ground state energy in quantum chemistry simulations. This estimation involves applying powers of a unitary to the ground state, controlled by an auxiliary state prepared on a control register. In many applications the goal is to provide a confidence interval for the phase estimate, and optimal performance is provided by a discrete prolate spheroidal sequence. We show how to prepare the corresponding state in a far more efficient way than prior work. We find that a matrix product state representation with a bond dimension of 4 is sufficient to give a highly accurate approximation for all dimensions tested, up to [MATH]. This matrix product state can be efficiently prepared using a sequence of simple three-qubit operations. When the dimension is a power of 2, the phase estimation can be performed with only three qubits for the control register, making it suitable for early-generation fault-tolerant quantum computers with a limited number of logical qubits.

﻿

.
tldr: The paper shows how to efficiently prepare the optimal discrete prolate spheroidal sequence state for quantum phase estimation using a bond-dimension-4 matrix product state, enabling implementation with only three control qubits.
motivation: Quantum phase estimation is central to quantum algorithms such as ground-state energy estimation in quantum chemistry, and achieving an optimal confidence interval typically requires preparing a discrete prolate spheroidal sequence state that is expensive to create.
method: The authors approximate the optimal phase-estimation control state by a matrix product state of bond dimension 4, verified accurate across all dimensions tested, and give an efficient preparation circuit built from simple three-qubit operations.
result: The MPS representation achieves high accuracy for all tested dimensions, and when the dimension is a power of 2 the control register requires only three qubits, drastically reducing logical-qubit overhead.
conclusion: The approach makes optimal-confidence quantum phase estimation practical for early fault-tolerant quantum computers with limited numbers of logical qubits, though the contribution is an algorithmic/compilation improvement rather than an information-theoretic result.

title: Efficient Graph State Generation In Linear Optics
authors: Seungbeom Chin And William John Munro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2189 (2026).

Graph states are central resources for quantum information processing, supporting applications in computation, communication, and error correction. In photonic systems, they are typically assembled from smaller entangled states using probabilistic fusion gates, which demand many photons and suffer from low success rates. We present an optimized scheme for directly generating caterpillar graph states (CGSs)—essential resource states for constructing high-dimensional lattice graph states—using only single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements. Based on the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, our method produces CGSs efficiently. For CGSs of length [MATH], it requires [MATH] fewer photons and achieves a success rate [MATH] times higher than fusion-based approaches. These results demonstrate that the LQG picture provides a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states for efficient quantum information processing.

.
tldr: The paper presents an optimized linear-optics scheme for directly generating caterpillar graph states (CGSs) using single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements, saving photons and boosting success rates versus fusion-based assembly.
motivation: Photonic graph states are key resources for quantum computation, communication, and error correction, but conventional probabilistic fusion-gate assembly is photon-hungry and inefficient, motivating a direct generation approach.
method: Building on the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, the authors design a scheme that directly produces caterpillar graph states—the building blocks for high-dimensional lattice graph states—using only single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements.
result: For CGSs of length M, the scheme requires substantially fewer photons and achieves a success rate orders of magnitude higher than fusion-based approaches.
conclusion: The LQG picture offers a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states for efficient quantum information processing, though the work sits in photonic computing hardware rather than the researcher's core theoretical directions.

title: On The Quantum Computational Complexity Of Classical Linear Dynamics With Geometrically Local Interactions: Dequantization And Universality
authors: Kazuki Sakamoto And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2182 (2026).

The simulation of large-scale classical systems in exponentially small space on quantum computers has gained attention. The prior work demonstrated that a quantum algorithm offers an exponential speedup over any classical algorithm in simulating classical dynamics with long-range interactions. However, many real-world classical systems, such as those arising from partial differential equations, exhibit only local interactions. The question remains whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition. In this work, we thoroughly characterize the computational complexity of simulating such geometrically local systems on quantum computers. First, we dequantize the quantum algorithm for simulating short-time (polynomial-time) dynamics of such systems. This implies that the problem of simulating this dynamics does not yield any exponential quantum advantage. Second, we show that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Third, we show that the computational complexity of simulating long-time (exponential-time) dynamics is captured by exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation. This suggests a super-polynomial time advantage when restricting the computation to polynomial-space, or an exponential space advantage otherwise. This work offers new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations, providing a pathway for achieving quantum advantage in practical problems.

.
tldr: The paper dequantizes quantum algorithms for short-time simulation of geometrically local classical linear dynamics and shows long-time simulation is captured by exponential-space quantum computation.
motivation: Many classical systems governed by partial differential equations have only local interactions, and it was unclear whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition.
method: The authors analyze the computational complexity of simulating geometrically local classical linear dynamics on quantum computers, dequantizing the short-time quantum algorithm and comparing complexity classes.
result: Short-time dynamics yields no exponential quantum advantage and is at least as hard as polynomial-time linear-space probabilistic classical computation, while long-time dynamics is captured by exponential-time polynomial-space quantum computation.
conclusion: The work provides new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations and suggests pathways for quantum advantage in practical problems.

title: Structured Flows Regulate Droplet Dynamics In Phase-separating Fluids
authors: Yulin Li, Tong Zhou, Yanyu Li, Qi Zhang And Zhihong You
abstract: Liquid–liquid phase separation is a fundamental route by which homogeneous fluids self-organize into mesoscale droplets and domains. In passive mixtures, the fate of these structures is largely dictated by curvature-dependent chemical potentials, which drive interfacial relaxation and Ostwald ripening toward progressively coarser morphologies. Here we show that structured flows can drive phase-separating fluids into flow-selected nonequilibrium states, thereby qualitatively rewriting the droplet dynamics. Using an advective Cahn–Hilliard model, we demonstrate that patterned velocity fields deform droplet interfaces along the streamlines of the imposed flow. The resulting curvature variations reshape the chemical-potential landscape that steers diffusive material transport. The resulting fluxes allow structured vortices to capture droplets, select stable droplet sizes, and invert the conventional ripening hierarchy by rendering larger droplets effectively less stable than smaller ones. In many-droplet systems, periodic and disordered vortex fields arrest coarsening and select steady morphologies whose length scales and symmetries are set by the underlying flow structure. Together, these results establish structured flow as a nonequilibrium route for controlling the thermodynamic driving forces that govern phase-separating fluids.
tldr: Structured flows can select nonequilibrium droplet states in phase-separating fluids, arresting coarsening and inverting the usual ripening hierarchy.
motivation: Liquid–liquid phase separation typically coarsens via Ostwald ripening, but external flows may reshape the thermodynamic driving forces and stabilize droplet patterns.
method: The authors use an advective Cahn–Hilliard model with imposed patterned velocity fields to simulate how flow streamlines deform droplet interfaces and alter diffusive material transport.
result: Vortex fields capture droplets, select stable sizes, and make larger droplets less stable than smaller ones, while periodic or disordered vortices arrest coarsening and set steady morphologies.
conclusion: Structured flow provides a nonequilibrium route to control phase-separating fluids and their thermodynamic driving forces, with implications for pattern formation in soft matter.

title: Measuring Universal Magnetocaloric Scaling Functions Near Quantum Critical Point
authors: Junsen Xiang, Enze Lv, Qinxin Shen, Cheng Su, Xuetong He, Yinghao Zhu, Yuan Gao, Xin-Yang Liu, Dai-Wei Qu, Xinlei Wang, Xi Chen, Qian Zhao, Haifeng Li, Shuo Li, Jie Yang, Jun Luo, Wentao Jin, Yang Qi, Rui Zhou, Wei Li, Peijie Sun And Gang Su
abstract: Near a quantum critical point (QCP), the low-temperature thermodynamics follows universal scaling laws. Using copper sulfate pentahydrate—a canonical spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain compound—we report the observation of a universal magnetocaloric effect (MCE) near a field-driven QCP. Remarkably, in the 1D quantum-critical regime, we obtain the universal magnetocaloric scaling function via adiabatic demagnetization measurements, which agrees with the analytical solution of the critical 1D Fermi gas. This establishes the copper sulfate crystal as an ideal platform for studying quantum criticality and universal phenomena. Upon further cooling, our MCE and nuclear magnetic resonance measurements reveal a dimensional crossover to a 3D quantum-critical regime of the Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC) universality class, characterized by the scaling law and a clear data collapse of the magnetic Grüneisen ratio with the 3D Bose-gas scaling function . Practically, this quantum-critical MCE enables cooling to 68.7 mK near the QCP and achieves a lowest temperature of 12.8 mK at zero field without the need for helium-3. Our work identifies a universal MCE in a common compound, establishing this magnon BEC system as a prototype quantum-critical coolant and a platform for next-generation millikelvin refrigeration.
tldr: The paper reports the observation of a universal magnetocaloric scaling function near a field-driven quantum critical point in copper sulfate pentahydrate, revealing a dimensional crossover to 3D Bose-Einstein condensation universality.
motivation: Near a quantum critical point, low-temperature thermodynamics is expected to follow universal scaling laws, but direct measurements of universal magnetocaloric scaling functions have been lacking.
method: Adiabatic demagnetization measurements and nuclear magnetic resonance were used on a spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain compound to probe the magnetocaloric effect across the quantum critical regime.
result: The extracted 1D scaling function agrees with the critical Fermi gas solution, and further cooling reveals a crossover to a 3D Bose-gas scaling function; the effect enables cooling to 68.7 mK near the QCP and 12.8 mK at zero field without helium-3.
conclusion: The work identifies a universal magnetocaloric effect in a common compound and establishes a magnon Bose-Einstein condensate system as a prototype quantum-critical coolant for millikelvin refrigeration.

title: Topological Phase And Its Effective Tuning In A Ladder Lattice
authors: Qi-Bo Zeng
abstract: We study a two-leg ladder model consisting of a one-dimensional (1D) Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) lattice with staggered nearest-neighboring hopping amplitudes and a normal 1D tight-binding lattice with uniform hopping. By varying the strength of inter-leg coupling, we find that topologically nontrivial phase with zero-energy edge modes will emerge, even when the SSH leg is in the trivial regime. Compared with the single SSH model, the nontrivial region in the parameter space is significantly expanded in the ladder. The topological phase is characterized by quantized Berry phase, and the phase boundaries are determined analytically. We also analyze the distributions of topological zero modes in the ladder, and find that the nontrivial regime can be further divided into two regions, which are separated by a gap closing point in the energy spectrum and correspond to the cases with edge modes residing in different legs. These results indicate that the topological phase and edge modes can be effectively tuned through the manipulations in the trivial lattice. Our work unveils the emergence of nontrivial topology in the ladder lattices and provides a new platform for studying topological phases.
tldr: A two-leg ladder combining an SSH chain and a trivial tight-binding chain exhibits an expanded topological phase with tunable zero-energy edge modes controlled by inter-leg coupling.
motivation: Topological phases in simple ladder geometries could provide new platforms for studying edge states, but the interplay between a trivial leg and a topological leg remains less explored.
method: The authors analyze a two-leg ladder with staggered hopping on one leg and uniform hopping on the other, using Berry phase and analytic phase-boundary calculations to characterize the topological phase and edge-mode distributions.
result: They find that nontrivial topology with zero-energy edge modes emerges even when the SSH leg is trivial, with the topological region expanded and split into two subregions separated by a gap closing.
conclusion: The topological phase and edge modes can be effectively tuned via the trivial lattice, offering a platform for topological phase studies.

title: Symmetry-free Quantum-dot Metasurfaces Realize Arbitrary Polarization-direction Emission
authors: Jiazheng Qin, Zhou Zhou, Jianfeng Chen, Zhe Wang, Xinyu Wang, Zhaogang Dong, Yan Liu, Li Jun Lim, Jiangang Feng, Weijin Chen, Jin Hong Ng, Chang Hoong Chow, Victor Leong, Shuihua Yang, Xuan Dong, Yuzhi Shi, Zhi-Kuang Tan And Cheng-Wei Qiu
abstract: Emission from quantum dots (QDs) is inherently broadband, isotropic, and unpolarized, exhibiting poor spatial and temporal coherence that largely limits their applications in directional and polarization-controlled light sources. While resonant metasurfaces supporting symmetry-protected BICs can enhance emission through high-Q radiative resonances near the BIC in momentum space, their rigid symmetries confine emission to fixed directions and polarization states, preventing robust emission control. Here, we overcome the symmetry-imposed limitations by introducing a symmetry-free resonant metasurface that transforms incoherent QD emission into multiple directional illuminations with designable polarizations and enhanced spatial and temporal coherence. Our recipe allows continuous and robust control of emission while preserving resonance quality. Our approach unifies coherence enhancement and emission shaping within a unified framework, establishing a scalable and versatile platform for active photonic chips and tunable quantum light sources.
tldr: A symmetry-free quantum-dot metasurface transforms incoherent QD emission into multiple directional beams with designable polarizations and enhanced coherence.
motivation: Quantum dot emission is inherently broadband, isotropic, and unpolarized, limiting its use in directional and polarization-controlled light sources; existing symmetry-protected BIC metasurfaces restrict emission to fixed directions and polarizations.
method: The authors design a symmetry-free resonant metasurface that couples to QD emission, enabling continuous and robust control over emission direction and polarization while preserving high resonance quality.
result: The platform converts incoherent QD emission into multiple directional illuminations with designable polarizations and simultaneously enhances spatial and temporal coherence.
conclusion: This approach unifies coherence enhancement and emission shaping, offering a scalable and versatile platform for active photonic chips and tunable quantum light sources.

title: Solving The Nonlinear Vlasov Equation On A Quantum Computer
authors: Tamás Vaszary, Animesh Datta, Tom Goffrey, And Brian Appelbe
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2206 (2026).

The practical applicability of a recent Carleman-linearization-based quantum algorithm for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with quadratic nonlinearities is investigated for the nonlinear electrostatic Vlasov equation with Krook-type collision operators. The equation is discretized on a (1+1)-dimensional phase-space grid and mapped onto the input of the quantum algorithm.
